about.title: David Faham
about.lead: A born-and-raised New Yorker and the founder of Faham Law LLC. Since 2011, he has advised businesses of every size, from founders forming their first company to established companies, on the legal work that keeps them growing.
bio: David serves as fractional general counsel to privately held companies, handling the contracts, employment questions, compliance and day-to-day legal decisions that an in-house lawyer would. Having served as general counsel for companies large and small, he brings that perspective to outside counsel work: practical advice that fits how a business actually runs.

His practice also covers the transactions those companies run into. He helps entrepreneurs start new businesses, handling entity formation, operating agreements, website terms, and SaaS and end-user agreements. He represents buyers and sellers in mergers and acquisitions, with transactions ranging from a few hundred thousand to a few million dollars. He handles commercial and residential real estate transactions, including closings and lease reviews. And he protects intellectual property, from trademark searches and filings through registration, maintenance and renewals.
Clients include consumer products and wholesale companies, licensing companies, technology companies and startups, restaurants, apparel brands, Amazon and e-commerce sellers, and real estate clients.
about.personal: David is a father of four and when work and family are not the priority, enjoys bowling in a local league and considers himself a foodie and scotch and wine aficionado.

faqs.q: What does a fractional general counsel do?
faqs.a: The same work as an in-house lawyer, on a part-time basis: contracts, employment questions, compliance, managing outside counsel and advice on business decisions.

faqs.q: Is that the same as outside general counsel?
faqs.a: Yes. "Fractional" and "outside" general counsel are two names for the same arrangement: an outside lawyer who serves as your company's general counsel part time, instead of a full-time in-house hire.

Most clients use a monthly retainer sized to the scope of their everyday legal needs. We quote it after a consultation, once we understand your business. Work outside the retainer, and matter-by-matter work, is billed at $495 per hour or on a flat fee where the matter allows.

faqs.q: Can we start with a single matter?
faqs.a: Yes. Many retainer clients started with one contract or one employment question. If the relationship makes sense for both sides, we move to a retainer from there.

faqs.q: How much does a trademark application cost?
faqs.a: Our fee for a standard U.S. application is $995, plus the USPTO filing fee of $350 per class. Searches, office action responses and renewals are listed on our fee schedule.

faqs.q: How long does trademark registration take?
faqs.a: The USPTO reports an average of about 10 months from filing, depending on its backlog and whether the examiner raises issues.

faqs.q: When do I need to renew?
faqs.a: A maintenance declaration is due between the 5th and 6th year after registration, then a combined declaration and renewal every 10 years.

faqs.q: Do I need a trademark for Amazon Brand Registry?
faqs.a: Yes. Amazon requires a pending application or an active registration for a word mark, or a design mark that includes words, from a government trademark office, and the trademark owner must be the one who enrolls. Filing the application is the first step.

faqs.q: Should I form an LLC or a corporation?
faqs.a: It depends on how you plan to raise money, pay yourself and handle taxes. Many small businesses start as LLCs, and companies planning to raise venture capital often form corporations.

faqs.q: Do I need an operating agreement?
faqs.a: New York requires LLCs to adopt a written operating agreement. Even where it isn't required, it sets out who owns what and what happens if a member leaves.

faqs.q: What is New York's LLC publication requirement?
faqs.a: New York LLCs must publish notice of formation in two newspapers within 120 days of forming, or lose the authority to do business in the state until they comply.

Across our practice, we advise clients in deals ranging from a few hundred thousand to a few million dollars.

practices.who: Owners selling their businesses, companies buying competitors or suppliers, and partners buying each other out, across consumer products, wholesale, technology, restaurants, apparel and e-commerce.

faqs.q: What's the difference between an asset sale and a stock sale?
faqs.a: In an asset sale the buyer picks which assets and liabilities it takes. In a stock sale the buyer takes the whole company, including its liabilities. Each choice has different tax and risk consequences.

faqs.q: Is a letter of intent binding?
faqs.a: Usually only in part. Price and deal terms are often non-binding, while confidentiality and exclusivity provisions typically are binding.

faqs.q: What is attorney review in New Jersey?
faqs.a: In New Jersey, a residential contract prepared by a real estate agent has a three-business-day attorney review period, during which either side's attorney can approve, change or cancel it.

faqs.q: Should a lawyer review my commercial lease?
faqs.a: Yes. Commercial leases are usually drafted for the landlord, and terms like rent increases, repairs, personal guarantees and early exit are negotiable before you sign.
It depends on your lease. Most commercial leases require the landlord's written consent, and some prohibit subleasing outright.
